title: Restorative and Conservative Dentistry
description: Diagnosis and treatment planning, minimal intervention cavity preparation, direct restorations, endodontics, crowns and bridges, and tooth wear and aesthetics.

topics.title: Diagnosis, Treatment Planning and Minimal Intervention
topics.summary: History and examination, caries risk assessment, radiographs and minimal intervention dentistry.

notes.b: Restorative care begins with a thorough history (complaint, medical history — anticoagulants, bisphosphonates, cardiac conditions, diabetes, pregnancy, HIV; dental history, diet, habits) and examination (extraoral, soft tissues, periodontal screening with BPE, teeth — caries, restorations, wear, mobility; occlusion). Pulp sensibility tests (cold — ethyl chloride or refrigerant spray; electric pulp test) and percussion help diagnose pulp and periapical status. Radiographs: bitewings (interproximal caries and bone levels), periapicals (roots, periapical tissues), OPG (overview — third molars, pathology). Caries risk assessment (diet, fluoride exposure, plaque, saliva, previous caries, social factors) determines recall intervals and preventive intensity. Treatment planning follows phases: relief of pain and emergency care, disease control (oral hygiene, diet, caries stabilisation, periodontal therapy), definitive restorative care, and maintenance.

Minimal intervention dentistry (MID) emphasises prevention, early detection and remineralisation of non-cavitated lesions (fluoride varnish, toothpaste, diet change), preserving tooth structure, and repairing rather than replacing defective restorations. Selective caries removal: remove soft infected dentine peripherally to achieve a sound margin for sealing but leave firm/leathery dentine over the pulp in deep lesions to avoid pulp exposure (reduces pulp exposure versus complete removal). Sealing caries (fissure sealants, Hall technique crowns in primary molars) arrests lesions by depriving bacteria of substrate. Atraumatic restorative treatment (ART) with hand instruments and high-viscosity glass ionomer suits community settings in Nigeria without electricity. Silver diamine fluoride (SDF) arrests caries non-invasively (stains lesions black). Cavity design has moved from G.V. Black's 'extension for prevention' to adhesive, conservative preparations.

topics.title: Direct Restorations
topics.summary: Amalgam and composite techniques, matrix systems, moisture control and restoration failure.

notes.b: Moisture control (rubber dam — gold standard for adhesive restorations and endodontics; cotton rolls, saliva ejectors) is essential. Amalgam preparation requires mechanical retention (undercuts, grooves), sufficient bulk (at least 1.5–2 mm), and a 90° cavosurface margin (butt joint); it is condensed incrementally, carved and burnished. Composite restorations use adhesive bonding with bevelled enamel margins (anterior), incremental placement (≤ 2 mm layers) to reduce polymerisation shrinkage stress, adequate light curing, and finishing and polishing. Matrix systems (Tofflemire, sectional matrices with rings) and wedges restore proximal contour and contact points, preventing overhangs and food packing. Glass ionomer is ideal for cervical lesions, high-caries-risk patients and primary teeth; the sandwich (layered) technique combines GIC base with composite. Shade selection under natural light before rubber dam isolation (teeth dehydrate and lighten).
k: GIC for cervical and high risk

notes.b: Restoration failure causes: secondary (recurrent) caries at margins (the most common reason for replacement), fracture of restoration or tooth (cuspal fracture — consider cuspal coverage for teeth with large restorations or after root canal treatment), marginal breakdown, wear, discolouration, and postoperative sensitivity (from polymerisation shrinkage, microleakage, occlusal high spots, or pulpal inflammation). Assessment of existing restorations uses criteria such as marginal integrity, anatomy, secondary caries and aesthetics (FDI criteria). Repair rather than replacement conserves tooth structure when feasible. Amalgam alternatives are promoted under the Minamata Convention phase-down, with restrictions for children under 15 and pregnant women in many jurisdictions. Cracked tooth syndrome causes sharp pain on biting (especially on release) — diagnosed with bite tests and transillumination; treat with cuspal coverage restorations.

topics.title: Endodontics
topics.summary: Pulp therapy, root canal treatment steps, irrigation, obturation and outcomes.

notes.b: Vital pulp therapy preserves pulp vitality: indirect pulp capping, direct pulp capping of small exposures (calcium silicate cements such as MTA or Biodentine preferred over calcium hydroxide), and pulpotomy (removing inflamed coronal pulp — increasingly used even for irreversible pulpitis in mature teeth; standard in primary molars). Root canal treatment (RCT) is indicated for irreversible pulpitis, pulp necrosis and apical periodontitis in restorable teeth. Steps: diagnosis and preoperative radiograph, local anaesthesia, rubber dam isolation (mandatory — prevents contamination and inhalation of files), access cavity (remove the entire roof of the pulp chamber — straight-line access), locating canals (e.g. second mesiobuccal canal in upper first molars; lower incisors may have two canals), working length determination (electronic apex locator and radiograph — about 0.5–1 mm short of the radiographic apex), cleaning and shaping (hand or rotary nickel–titanium files; crown-down), irrigation, and obturation.

Irrigation disinfects the canal system that files cannot reach: sodium hypochlorite (0.5–5.25% — dissolves organic tissue, antibacterial; extrusion beyond the apex causes a painful 'hypochlorite accident' with swelling and bruising), EDTA (removes the smear layer), and chlorhexidine; activation (sonic or ultrasonic) improves efficacy. Intracanal medicament (calcium hydroxide) between visits. Obturation with gutta-percha and sealer (cold lateral condensation or warm vertical techniques) to seal the canal; then a coronal seal — definitive restoration (cuspal coverage for posterior teeth) promptly to prevent coronal leakage, a major cause of failure. Outcome assessment by clinical signs and radiographic periapical healing at 1 year and beyond; failure may require non-surgical retreatment or surgical endodontics (apicectomy). Procedural errors: ledges, perforations, file separation, and missed canals. Immature teeth with necrotic pulps: apexification (MTA plug) or regenerative endodontics.

topics.title: Crowns, Bridges and Indirect Restorations
topics.summary: Indications, tooth preparation, materials, impressions and replacing missing teeth with bridges.

notes.b: Indications for crowns: heavily restored or fractured teeth, root-canal-treated posterior teeth (cuspal protection), aesthetics (discoloured or malformed teeth), and bridge retainers. Materials: full metal (gold or base metal — minimal reduction), metal–ceramic (porcelain fused to metal), all-ceramic (lithium disilicate — excellent aesthetics; zirconia — high strength, posterior use), and composite. Principles of preparation: preservation of tooth structure, retention and resistance form (taper of about 6° total, adequate height), structural durability (adequate reduction — e.g. 1.5–2 mm occlusal for metal–ceramic), marginal integrity (chamfer or shoulder finish lines) and preservation of the periodontium (supragingival margins where possible). Posts and cores restore endodontically treated teeth with insufficient coronal structure; a ferrule (at least 1.5–2 mm of sound tooth encircled by the crown) reduces fracture risk. Impressions (addition silicone, digital scans), provisional crowns, occlusal registration, try-in and cementation follow.

Fixed partial dentures (bridges) replace missing teeth: conventional (full-coverage retainers on prepared abutments — fixed–fixed, cantilever), and resin-bonded (minimal-preparation adhesive bridges with metal wings — conservative, ideal for replacing single anterior teeth in young patients). Abutment evaluation: periodontal support, crown–root ratio, root form, vitality and position; Ante's law (the root surface area of abutments should equal or exceed that of the teeth being replaced) is a guideline. Pontic designs: ridge-lap, modified ridge-lap (anterior aesthetics), hygienic/sanitary (posterior mandible), ovate. Cleaning under pontics with superfloss or interdental brushes is essential. Alternatives: removable partial dentures (common and affordable in Nigeria) and dental implants (growing availability, cost is a barrier). Complications: caries under retainers, debonding, loss of vitality of abutments, and periodontal disease.

topics.title: Tooth Wear, Hypersensitivity and Aesthetic Dentistry
topics.summary: Erosion, attrition, abrasion, dentine hypersensitivity, discolouration and bleaching.

notes.b: Tooth wear (non-carious tooth surface loss): erosion (acid — soft drinks, citrus, vomiting in eating disorders or pregnancy, gastro-oesophageal reflux — smooth, cupped lesions, palatal surfaces of upper incisors with reflux/vomiting), attrition (tooth-to-tooth — bruxism; flat facets matching opposing teeth), abrasion (external objects — incorrect horizontal toothbrushing, chewing sticks used vigorously — notched cervical lesions), and abfraction (flexural stress — wedge-shaped cervical lesions). Management: identify and remove the cause (diet advice, reflux treatment, occlusal splints for bruxism, brushing technique), monitor (study models, photographs, indices), fluoride, and restore when necessary (composite additions, Dahl technique for localised anterior wear). Dentine hypersensitivity: short sharp pain from exposed dentine to thermal, tactile or osmotic stimuli (hydrodynamic theory) — desensitising toothpastes (potassium nitrate, stannous fluoride, arginine), fluoride varnish, bonding agents, and treating causes (gingival recession, wear).

Tooth discolouration: extrinsic (tea, coffee, tobacco, kola nut chewing — common in parts of Nigeria, chlorhexidine; removed by scaling and polishing) and intrinsic (fluorosis — mottling in high-fluoride areas; tetracycline — grey–brown banding; trauma and pulp necrosis — dark single tooth; dentinogenesis imperfecta; ageing). Treatment options: external vital bleaching (carbamide peroxide 10% in custom trays; hydrogen peroxide in-office — sensitivity is common; regulated concentrations), internal ('walking') bleaching for root-filled discoloured teeth (with a cervical seal to prevent external cervical resorption), microabrasion for superficial fluorosis, resin infiltration, composite or porcelain veneers, and crowns. Informed consent, realistic expectations and minimal invasiveness guide aesthetic dentistry; smile analysis considers the smile line, midline, proportions and gingival display.
